en: *Ji shamen buying baisu dengshi* (Collected Matters on Why Śramaṇas Should Not Bow to the Laity), Scroll One, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Yancong of Hongfu Monastery.
Section One: Accounts of the Past (1–2). Part One: Upper. Section One: Accounts of the Past, Part One, Upper.
The "Preface to Past Events" clarifies matters such as the practice of śramaṇas paying homage during the period prior to the Sui dynasty.
Since the Great Dharma flowed eastward more than six hundred years ago, [this account has been compiled].
Within this, faith and slander alternate, and praise and disparagement contend;
it repeatedly causes defilement and ruin, and frequently compels prostration.
Yet these matters do not accord with the governance of the state, and their principles transcend the natural order of Heaven.
This was used as a pretext to undermine the Way [of the Buddha],
and both sides persisted in following the old precedents.
[Attached are] three memorials submitted by He Chong and others, Ministers of the Imperial Secretariat of the Jin Dynasty, regarding the petition that śramaṇas should not pay homage to the sovereign.
Preface to the Two Imperial Edicts Issued by Emperor Cheng to the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Yu Bing, Ordering Śramaṇas to Pay Homage (2);
Letter with Preface from the Grand Marshal Huan Xuan to the Eight Ministers, including Huan Qian, Concerning the Matter of Whether Monastics Should Pay Homage (1);
and the Reply from the Eight Ministers and Others to Huan Xuan Clarifying that Monastics Should Not Pay Homage (1).
One letter by Huan Xuan to Wang Mi, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, concerning the matter of whether śramaṇas should pay homage;
one letter by Wang Mi in reply to Huan Xuan clarifying that śramaṇas should not pay homage; three treatises refuting Huan Xuan’s arguments against Wang Mi’s position that they should not pay homage;
and three letters by Wang Mi in reply to Huan Xuan’s rebuttals regarding the necessity of paying homage.
A letter by Huan Xuan to Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, setting forth the reasons why *śramaṇas* do not pay homage to the sovereign;
two letters exchanged between Huiyuan and Huan Xuan;
and three memorials submitted by He Chong and others, Minister of the Imperial Secretariat of the Jin Dynasty, asserting that *śramaṇas* should not pay homage to the sovereign.
Preface: In the sixth year of the Xiánkāng era of the Eastern Jin dynasty, Emperor Cheng was still a minor;
at that time, the Empress Dowager presided over the court and governed the state.

Wang Dao, the Minister of Education and Director of the Secretariat, served alongside his father-in-law Yu Liang, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, to assist in the administration of state affairs.
Later, after Wang Dao and the others passed away,
Yu Bing took charge of the government.
It was said that all śramaṇas ought to pay full respect to the king.
Lü Chang and others argued that they should not pay such respect.
The Minister of Rites was ordered to deliberate on the matter in detail; the *boshi* (doctors) and others reached a conclusion identical to that of Lü Chang.
The Gate Secretariat received the imperial decree and drafted a rebuttal;
consequently, Chong and others submitted this memorial.
This was the initial petition.
Shangshu Ling, General of the Chariot and Cavalry, Pacifier of the Army, and Duke of Duxiang;
Your Servant, the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Left Vice Director, Count of Changping;
and Your Servant, the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Right Vice Director, Count of Jian’an.
The Grand Scribe, His Majesty’s Subject Huai, Guardian of the Marquisate of Guanzhong;
the Grand Scribe, His Majesty’s Subject Guang, Son of the Marquis of Chang’an, and others, state:
Emperor Wu, the Martial Ancestor, established a new dynasty through his supreme brilliance and sagacity.
Our late Emperor Ming, the Ancestor Su, was sagacious and possessed profound insight.
How could he have forced those śramaṇas who do not conform to the times to bow their knees?
He merely took into account that they would not change their methods for cultivating goodness.
This is how one penetrates the wills of all under heaven.
I, the humble writer, believe it would be most appropriate to follow the precedents established by the late Emperor;
in principle, this is the superior course.

The General of Chariots and Cavalry, Yu Bing, issued an edict on behalf of Emperor Cheng requiring śramaṇas to pay homage; two edicts issued by Yu Bing on behalf of Emperor Cheng requiring śramaṇas to pay homage. First Edict.
Now, the myriad regions have diverse customs and the Way of the Spirits is difficult to discern;
this has been so from time immemorial. For one who possesses a comprehensive perspective and universal understanding, it is truly not to be wondered at.
How much more so regarding the rites of kneeling and prostrating;
why must one necessarily adhere to them?
One should instead first investigate the underlying intention of the former kings for which they esteemed these practices.
How could it be that one merely delights in these contortions and sits encountering such awkward postures? Certainly not;
it is because of the reverence due between father and son.
To establish the order between ruler and subject,
to formulate laws and regulations, and to honor the ranks of ritual—
how could these be for nothing?
There is indeed a reason for this.
Since there is a reason,
by what means could it be changed?
If this is so, then is the establishment of names and rituals devoid of reality?
Moreover, do you truly intend to say that there is a Buddha?
Is there no Buddha?
Is there a Buddha?
His Way is indeed vast.
If there is no Buddha,
on what basis can one maintain the continuity of faith?
Nevertheless, this is a matter beyond the mundane world.
Matters beyond the mundane world are not something to be realized within the mundane realm;
one must therefore transcend the physical form and depart from ordinary affairs.
That the *Yili* (Book of Rites) discards the teachings of names (*mingjiao*) is what I find most deeply suspicious.
The teachings of names have a long historical origin.
It has not been abolished for a hundred generations.
Though the great manifestation [of the Way] occurred at the break of dawn, later ages have still remained in peril.
The cause of this perilous state of affairs is difficult to discern.
Now, you would instead aspire to the distant and obscure, following that which is hazy and indistinct, abandoning ritual in a single morning and discarding the teachings in this present age,
thereby causing the common masses to become arrogant and negligent toward the laws and regulations.
Furthermore, this is what I deeply doubt.
Even if it were truly so;
even if it actually existed.
I shall communicate this to the divine spirits;
it is simply a matter of attaining it within one's own breast.
This is the grand model of the guiding laws and regulations.
It is certainly not permissible to exclude such individuals from the formal court.
All these people are subjects of Jin;
when their talents and wisdom are considered, they are merely ordinary men.
Yet, because the principles to be explained were difficult to discern, he adopted provisional attire to cross over [the world];
he resisted the haughty rites of alien customs and presented his physical form directly before the Emperor.
Furthermore, this is something I would not accept.
You gentlemen are all men of state-caliber;
when it comes to profound discourse, you ought to fathom the subtle and the hidden.
In discussing governance, one ought to prioritize the national statutes;
if it were otherwise,
what would I have to recount?
Second Performance: Your Servant, Minister of the Secretariat, General of the Crown, Pacifier of the Army, and Marquis of Duchang, [Chen] Chong;
Your Servant, Attendant-at-the-Right, Left Vice-Director, and Viscount of Changping, [Chen] Xi;
Your Servant, Attendant-at-the-Right, Right Vice-Director, and Viscount of Jian'an, [Chen] Huai.
The Secretariat Official, Subject Huai, Marquis of Guanzhong, and the Secretariat Official, Subject Guang, Son of Chang’an, and others, state:
The imperial decree is as set forth above; we, your servants, are ignorant and deficient.
It is insufficient to praise the sacred intent and fully expound the great meaning.
Having humbly examined the brilliant edict,
I am struck with awe and tremble with apprehension.
We have repeatedly investigated and deliberated upon whether a Buddha exists or not;
truly, this is not something that we, your subjects, are capable of determining.
Nevertheless, we have examined his surviving writings and probed their essential tenets.
The prohibitions of the Five Precepts truly assist the King’s transformation of the people;
they value the hidden integrity of the unseen realm over the bright renown of manifest conduct.
The practice of virtue lies in forgetting the self.
Embracing the pure and wondrous state of single-mindedness,
this tradition has flourished from the Han dynasty down to the present day.
Although the Dharma may experience periods of flourishing and decline, it has never been tainted by such aberrant or delusory practices;
as for the Way of the Spirits,
there has never been its equal throughout the long course of history.
Now, while a curse may cause harm,
a blessing must surely bring benefit.
Such is my humble sincerity.
My sincere wish is that this tiny contribution of dust and dew may add moisture to the lofty peaks of Mount Song and Mount Dai;
that my humble prayers may, from above, assist the Imperial Ultimate.
Now, by ordering them to prostrate, you have utterly destroyed their Dharma.
It causes the common people who cultivate goodness to fall into neglect during the age of the sages;
when they practice what is real, it becomes their daily habit,
yet this inevitably leads to sorrow and fear, which they then conceal.
In my humble heart, I find this deeply unsettling.
Though I am ignorant and obscured,
how could I dare allow my biased views to mislead Your Majesty’s sagacious hearing?
I maintain that throughout the world’s three dynasties, successive generations have become increasingly enlightened and sagacious.
If we do not establish regulations for the present, there will be no deficiency in the royal law,
and the paths to the netherworld may remain free from congestion and obstruction.
For this reason, I again set forth my humble sincerity and beg for your gracious examination.
I respectfully submit this.
A further edict: I have carefully examined what you have presented and fully grasped its intent.
Matters that are profound and obscure truly cannot be exhausted by mere allegory.
However, this brief comparison represents the constant measure of the divine majesty of Great Beings;
it merely provides a rough outline of their respective categories.
Generally speaking, although the laws established by the hundred kings varied in their substance and form according to the times,
there has never been one who combined the customs of alien peoples with governance or blended such grandiose and heterodox transformations into the state.
Was it that the sages of old were not proficient in this?
Yet, how profoundly vast and comprehensive is the Sage of the Final Age!
Moreover, even the minor virtues of the five precepts roughly approximate the principles of human ethics.
Yet you have further abbreviated the rites of respect toward the Lord of the World?
The ritual is profound;
the reverence is great.
The essential principles for governing are fully contained herein.
It is not that the ruler of ten thousand chariots delights in being honored,
nor is it that the people within the realm delight in being humble.
If the distinction between the lowly and the honorable is not established, the royal teachings will fall into disorder;
this is why the ancient sages took the constitutional statutes as their model for governing the state—
a principle one ought not to doubt.
Those of versatile talent and broad learning often cultivate these qualities in their entirety.
It may be acceptable to cultivate them within one's own person and within one's family;
however, it is not permissible to cultivate them within a state or at court.
Is this not far from the truth?
Examining what you have presented, it appears you have indeed not yet understood the distinction between existence and non-existence.
Even if you were to understand it, you would still claim that it cannot be employed in governing.
How much more so when there is nothing at all—how could one then proceed south?
(Third Performance) Your Subjects, Chong and others, state:
Although we subjects are truly obscured by ignorance and fail to comprehend the profound intent, we...
As for being "ever-active and vigilant," one should think from dawn until night of following the royal ordinances;
how could one willfully cling to a partial perspective and thereby disrupt the great social relations?
It is simply because from the Han, Wei, and Jin dynasties onward, no dissenting opinions were heard;
the regulations governing the hierarchy of honor never suffered even a moment’s lapse.
Now, the śramaṇas are singularly diligent in observing their precepts.
Furthermore, their ritual observances are singular and uniform.
As for those who are steadfast in maintaining the precepts,
they do not begrudge even the sacrifice of their own bodies.
How could I dare to treat my physical form with such negligence as to disregard ritual reverence?
Whenever I see incense being burned and prayers being offered,
I invariably place the state first.
His desire for the magnification of blessings and his boundless affection were such that his supreme reverence and obedience arose spontaneously; thus,
his ritual observances were simplified.
This is because it is a method of single-mindedly upholding the Dharma.
Therefore, when the former sages governed the world,
they relied upon it.
Yet it has not been revoked.
The net of Heaven is vast and wide; though its mesh is coarse, nothing escapes it.
Your servants have repeatedly considered that this would not constitute a failure to pay our respects, nor would it violate the law.
Bestowing benefits according to what each person requires so that neither the wise nor the ignorant dare not employ their sincere hearts—
this constitutes the sovereign’s grace of supporting all like heaven and bearing all like earth.
Below, there is a person who maintains the One and cultivates goodness;
I respectfully present my humble and shallow thoughts once more,
hoping they may receive your examination and consideration.
Respectfully submitted. At that time, Yu Bing’s proposal was shelved, and in the end, no salutation was performed.

A letter by Huan Xuan, Grand Marshal, in discussion with the Eight Ministers including Huan Qian et al., regarding the matter of whether monastics should perform salutations; one letter with preface, from the Yuanxing era of the Jin dynasty.
Emperor An was driven into exile abroad. Huan Xuan,
the Grand Marshal, wielding a power that could intimidate the sovereign,
sought to compel the monks to prostrate themselves before him.
Because he considered the old accounts concerning He and Yu to be incomplete in their reasoning,
he wrote to the Eight Ministers, saying:
"Xu bows twice and prostrates himself."
The eighth day is fast approaching.
Why is it that the former śramaṇas all failed to show respect to the king?
Although Yu has already discussed this matter, [the issue remains].
Both of them merely followed their own perspectives;
they did not yet yield to one another on the basis of principle.
Yu’s intention lay in honoring the sovereign.
Yet the underlying principles have not been fully exhausted;
how could one emerge from such partiality and belief to ultimately fall into confusion regarding names and essences?
Now, as for the Buddha’s transformation of beings:
Although one may expansively infer that which lies beyond the reach of sight and hearing from its vast and boundless nature,
reverent cultivation remains the fundamental principle; in this regard, there is no difference.
Indeed, that which is expected is quite different; reverence and respect should certainly not be abandoned.
Laozi places kings and lords among the "Three Greats. If one examines the basis for their being so esteemed, [it is because they sustain all things].
All these depend upon the means of sustaining life and its universal circulation;
how could it be that they are praised as being comparable to the Two Polarities solely because a sage occupies the throne?
It is because the great virtue of Heaven and Earth is said to be "Life."
The principle of penetrating through life and governing all things resides in the King;
therefore, his sacred vessel is honored and the rites toward it are truly profound.
How could this be merely a matter of empty veneration? The underlying meaning lies in the sovereign’s governance.
The very means by which śramaṇas sustain their lives are also daily employed for the sake of principle and destiny;
how could one receive their bounty while neglecting the rites due to them?
To receive their bounty while neglecting one's reverence is something that reason cannot tolerate and which the heart finds unsettling.
We should together seek the underlying intent of this momentous matter for a generation and further investigate it thoroughly until its full meaning is exhausted.
I hope you will be able to finalize the detailed determination by the eighth day.
Huan Xuan bows twice and prostrates himself.

Respectfully addressed to the Eight Ministers, etc., regarding the matter of the response to Huan Xuan concerning that those who clarify the Way (Ming Dao-ren) should not pay homage. This letter from the Eight Ministers, etc., in response to Huan Xuan regarding the matter of those who clarify the Way not paying homage, was written by Huan Qian, General of the Central Army, Minister of the Secretariat, and Marquis of Kai-guo in Yiyang, and others.
I am terrified of the penalty of death.
Having received your instructions,
you have commanded that śramaṇas pay their respects to the king.
Although He and Yu have discussed this, their intent has not been fully exhausted;
as this is a matter of great importance,
it ought to be handled with perfect propriety.
Truly, your elegant discourse is as you have stated.
Nevertheless, the Buddha-dharma and that of Yao and Confucius differ in their ultimate aims;
their rites and teachings are mutually inconsistent.
Ordinary people hold their hair and skin in high regard,
yet those [monastics] shave them off without hesitation;
they leave the household life and abandon their kin.
One does not regard the nourishment of the physical form as filial piety;
rather, one treats the body as mere earth and wood, severs desire, and ceases all competition.
One does not seek blessings for a single lifetime, but aims for them throughout ten thousand kalpas.
That which the world prizes, he has cast it all aside;
that which ritual and instruction deem important, he has entirely severed his intent toward them.
Yet, in serving his father and attending to his sovereign, he maintains the ultimate expression of natural affection.
Since he has already severed his ties of kinship and affection,
how could he possibly perform the rites due to a sovereign of ten thousand chariots?
His status naturally ought to be set aside.
Throughout the three dynasties, they left those who had severed their bonds to roam at will;
one should regard this as the manifestation of the boundless spiritual intelligence, which cannot be examined through the limits of sensory perception.
Beyond what can be seen and heard, there may well be another principle.
If we were now to require them to show such reverence,
I fear that those things requiring reform would be many, not merely the matter of bowing and rising.
Furthermore, when a sovereign honors the Dharma, it arises from a spirit of respect.
To believe in their principles yet change their outward forms is something the heart still finds difficult to comprehend; therefore,
one should simply accept them as they are.
This is truly an act of leniency.

His Majesty’s decree provides a distinct response to the Duke’s difficulties. Zhang Chang of Konggu is there; I imagine he has already consulted with you in person regarding his thoughts on the Way and its treasures.
All the monastics are fully capable of responding to your lofty principles.
Your humble servants are unacquainted with Buddhist principles;
we have spoken according to our own feelings.
We regret that this is insufficient for your perusal.
Qian and the others are terrified and await their death penalty.

This is the first letter by Huan Xuan to Wang Mi, the Director of the Secretariat, concerning the matter of whether śramaṇas should pay homage [to the sovereign]. In this letter, Huan Xuan argues that śramaṇas should maintain a posture of equality with the Supreme Sovereign.
This is indeed a matter that my heart finds uneasy.
The great affairs of this era ought to be fully discussed together.
I have now written this letter to the Eight Ministers.
I have already sent everything previously;
now I send this letter.
You are the one who ought to take charge of these matters.
I have belatedly heard your virtuous decree.

Attached is a letter by Wang Mi, General of the Household, Minister of Personnel, Director of the Secretariat, and Marquis of Wugang, in response to Huan Xuan’s clarification regarding the matter that *śramaṇas* should not pay homage. **Letter by Wang Mi in Response to Huan Xuan’s Clarification on the Matter that *Śramaṇas* Should Not Pay Homage** [The letter] begins: General of the Household, Minister of Personnel, Director of the Secretariat, and Marquis of Wugang, Wang Mi.
I am terrified of the penalty of death.
Having received your instructions,
I have learned that the Daoist practitioners prostrate themselves before the Most Honored One.
I have also seen your letter to the Eight Ministers and have fully received your lofty intent;
your proposal regarding the inclusion of the sound *rong* is both eloquent in expression and perfect in reasoning.
Recently, I have also heard a rough outline of your noble principles;
however, I have not yet been able to exhaustively investigate the two points regarding He and Yu,
and I regret that my understanding remains incomplete.
Thus, they treat these as two separate treatises,
failing to understand that they leak from partial views.
However, the teaching on the True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the locus of the mind of renunciation is an elegant instruction.
Now, the rise of the Buddha-dharma originated in India;
its fundamental principles are profound and remote,
making them difficult to express through words.
Since we have already entered the realm of teaching,
it may be briefly stated:
I believe that different regions possess distinct customs and traditions.
Although their personal inclinations may often differ,
as for the principles by which they govern their subjects,
there are none that are not necessarily the same.
Now, although the śramaṇas harbor deep reverence in their hearts,
they do not consider physical prostration to be the true form of ritual propriety;
while their traces fill the entire land, their aspirations transcend those within the mundane realm.
For this reason, the rulers of foreign lands have all humbled themselves in ritual propriety;
it is truly because where the Way resides, there is honor.
One does not judge its weight by the person.
Tracing the proclamation and spread of the Great Dharma, it has surely been for a long time;
more than four hundred years have passed, spanning three successive dynasties.
Although customs may shift and policies change,
the propagation [of the Way] remains no different;
is this not because a uniquely transcendent transformation has utility in the gradual molding of character?
Does the spirit of purity and frugality not contribute to a period of great peace?
Therefore, the sovereign, with hands folded in self-possession, feels no resentment toward his own humble quarters;
and the śramaṇa, preserving his true nature, harbors no self-doubt regarding his birth in this world.
I accept that the mastery of principles for the transformation of things rests with the sovereign.
Examining the convergence of these principles,
it is indeed as your esteemed argument maintains.
I have read your virtuous words three times and cannot stop myself;
though I wish to offer a response, my words find no resting place.
Yet I still consider that those whose achievements are supreme receive no reward.
Those whose kindness is profound forget even expressions of thanks;
though one might rise and bow a hundred times,
how could that ever suffice to repay the virtue of providing such comprehensive salvation?
Since Your Excellency has not forgotten me in your regard and has condescended to question me,
I have hastily set forth my humble views,
merely to ensure that no offense is caused to what you uphold.
I pray that you will not reject these words because of the person who speaks them.
As I prepare this petition, I am filled with anxiety and remorse;
I fear the penalty of death, Sengmi.
Huan Xuan’s Three Refutations of Wang Mi on the Matter of Not Rendering Salutation First Refutation:
Your letter states that although the intentions of śramaṇas are profound in their reverence...
"And yet, one does not consider the physical bowing to be the essence of ritual propriety. An objection is raised:
"In the reverence shown by śramaṇas, is it not the case that they all disregard outward form to preserve the mind?"
Their practice of repentance and prostration is likewise earnest in its ritual application;
from their teachers down to the senior monks (upādhyāya and sthavira), they bow and kneel before worldly people as well,
differing only slightly in their specific regulations.
Since you cannot forget your physical form there,
why do you suddenly neglect the ritual decorum here?
Furthermore, as for the principle of the Master:
To take the means for awakening as one's virtue:
since the Way of the Ruler brings all things to life, it is logically appropriate that its root be established therein;
this is the meaning of the "threefold relation."
Is this not indeed the ultimate of human feeling and reason? Your letter states:
"Among the rulers of foreign lands, there are none who do not humble themselves in courtesy;
this is truly because where the Way resides, there is honor."
"One does not judge lightness or gravity by the person. An objection states:
"The rulers of foreign lands are not appropriate subjects for analogy;
however, the emergence of Buddhism can also be understood through its underlying intent."
Is it not because the six barbarian tribes are haughty and powerful that [the Buddha] constantly employs instruction and transformation?
Thus, he extensively displays spiritual wonders so that they may be struck with awe and submit.
Once they have been brought to awe and submission...
Thereafter, one follows the established tracks.
This is merely a matter of great fear regarding spirits, ghosts, and the retribution of blessings;
how could it be the profound and wondrous Way of the宗 (Zong)?
When the Way is present, one is noble;
this will differ from your refined opinion.
How could it be that the Way is already fully contained within merely donning the dharma robes?
If you claim that only when the Way is present does one become noble, then as you say,
the Way of the Sage is the ultimate of all ways; thus,
the reverence between ruler and minister becomes even more profound than that prescribed by ritual.
If this were the case, then śramaṇas would not be held in reverence;
how could it be that the Dharma is esteemed for its presence? Your letter states:
"Four hundred years have passed, and three dynasties have succeeded one another."
Yet they propagate it without distinction.

Is this not because a uniquely transcendent transformation is utilized daily in the process of gradual cultivation, and a style of purity and frugality does no harm to a period of great prosperity? The objection states:
That it has not been altered throughout successive dynasties is no proof [of its antiquity]. Previously,
the people of Jin had almost no devotion to Buddhism.
The assembly of śramaṇas consists entirely of various Hu people;
furthermore, the King does not associate with them.
Therefore, it is permissible to allow them their own local customs and not subject them to restrictive regulations.
Now the Sovereign honors the Buddha and personally attends to religious rites;
these matters differ from those of the past.
How can we not ensure that his conduct has a standard, and that his daily life is pure and frugal, thereby providing assistance to the Teaching?
Everything is as you have said.
This is surely the merit of the Buddha-dharma;
it is not something contributed by the arrogance or boastfulness of śramaṇas.
Now, by being deeply sincere and reverent, will you not further thicken the favor [you receive]? Your letter states:
"Those whose merit is high are not rewarded;
those whose kindness is deep forget thanks."
"Though one may bow once and rise once more, how could this suffice to repay the grace of universal salvation? An objection states:
"Now, when the ultimate principle is reached, there is no recompense."
Truly, it is as the Tathāgata has intended.
However, since my feelings are rooted in the boundless (the mourning for parents), I respectfully follow them from the outset.
This is precisely why the sages established ritual codes based on human emotions.
Yet each has fulfilled their entrusted duty. If,
because the merit is profound and the kindness is heavy,
one must certainly omit formal expressions of thanks.
Is the virtue of Śākyamuni then profound,
or is it shallow? If it were shallow, [how could this be so?]
It is not appropriate to disrupt the great human relationships for the sake of minor paths.
If [the former] is profoundly heterodox,
how could it be that one is made to be solemn and respectful there, while one’s own reverence is allowed to slacken here?

Wang Mi’s Response to Huan Xuan’s “Difficulties Regarding the Obligation to Pay Homage”: Three Sections. Huan Xuan’s Initial Difficulties against Wang Mi; Wang Mi’s Initial Response to Huan Xuan’s First Response. The Difficulties state: [The first section of Wang Mi’s response follows. [The second section of Wang Mi’s response follows. [The third section of Wang Mi’s response follows. *Note: This entry provides the structural framework for the text as it appears in the *Gujin shu yao*. The actual content of the three sections of Wang Mi’s response would follow this introductory header.*
Regarding the reverence of śramaṇas, how could it be that they all disregard physical form while preserving the mind?
Their practice of repentance and prostration is also earnestly devoted to ritual action. Answer:
Now, the Way of the śramaṇa takes reverence as its primary principle;
yet, since the paths diverge, [the methods differ].
Since his sense of righteousness allowed for no submission or yielding,
even though the gravity of his kinship ties was profound,
he completely set aside the formalities of physical ritual.
The reason why śramaṇas honor their masters and elders and mutually revere one another is truly because,
when the fundamental goal is the same, the order between senior and junior is established;
and when there is a basis for mutual reliance, outward affairs accord with the inner mind.
Originally, although the Buddha-dharma is vast, it does not omit even small virtues;
the retribution for the merit of a single blade of grass will likewise respond accordingly.
Accumulate hairs and they form a mountain.
The meaning is thus clearly established. An objection is raised:
"If the Way of the Ruler is to give universal life, then by principle it should reside in its primary source;
such is the meaning of the 'threefold relationship'."
Is this not indeed the ultimate limit of both principle and emotion? I reply:
For the Way of the Sovereign pervades all life, its principle is identical to that of the creative transformation of Heaven and Earth;
in forging and molding and distributing the vital breaths, its merit is truly vast.
Yet, one has not yet expressed gratitude for what has been bestowed, nor has one found a way to express this sense of thankfulness at the fundamental principle; why is this?
It is truly because the profound source is dark and remote.
It is not something that can be raised by material forms;
its movement is pervasive and its principle is subtle—
how could it be recompensed by coarse traces?
Therefore, the Master said:
"One may cause people to follow [the Way],
but one cannot cause them to understand it."
This is what is meant by that. An objection is raised:
"The rulers of foreign lands are not appropriate subjects for comparison;
furthermore, the intent behind the rise of Buddhism can also be understood."
Is it not because the six barbarian tribes are arrogant and unruly, and cannot be transformed by ordinary teachings?
Therefore, one must extensively manifest spiritual wonders to cause them to stand in awe and submit. The answer is:
Indeed, the establishment of the divine way through teaching is truly difficult to explain through words alone; its meaning lies beyond verbal discourse.
To extensively display spiritual wonders and demonstrate retribution is the most substantial principle of cause and effect,
and the fundamental core of Buddhism.
If one now claims that the three periods of time are a fabrication and that sin and merit are a source of fear,
then one rejects what Śākyamuni has clarified.
It would likely leave nothing to which one could turn for refuge.
I have always held that the transformation brought about by the Duke of Zhou and Confucius was intended to remedy extreme decadence;
therefore, their words and traces were fully exhausted within the span of a single lifetime.

in the kindness of procreation, filial care through expression and nourishment is paramount.
Yet now, both the Buddhist and Daoist teachings have entirely reversed these principles.
They perform the ritual of equal greeting with emperors and kings,
and receive veneration from their own parents;
yet this generous tolerance has been maintained from antiquity down to the present age.
Tracing its profound significance, there is indeed a reason for this:
it is surely because shaving the head differs from wearing the ceremonial cap,
and the kāṣāya robe has no place among the insignia of official rank.
Those who have left the household life revere the Dharma and renounce worldly affairs;
how could they be bound by the formalities of the imperial court?
As for the profound teachings, their purity and emptiness, and the far-reaching, expansive style of the Way, [they transcend such constraints].
They exalted their own principles and did not bow before kings or lords;
there were even emperors and sovereigns to whom they would not act as subjects—
this is precisely what is meant by that.
Since the state already upholds his Way,
he has not bent his person; we hope that,
in accordance with the preceding chapter, you will not violate established precedent.
Respectfully Submitted for Deliberation.

A Memorial on the Discussion by Gao Yao-shang and Others, One Chapter: The Dharma-source is profoundly quiescent and beyond names or words;
the Ultimate Way is subtle and ineffable, thus devoid of sound or teaching.
As for the realm of the three thousand great chiliocosms...
Those of limited wisdom cannot fathom its source;
within this state of vagueness and obscurity,
even the most eminent sages are unable to exhaustively investigate its principle.
However, the two masters, Śākyamuni and Laozi,
displayed the bearing of great sages;
their wisdom shone beyond the mundane world, transcending all things.
With the stone-sweeping of his short triple-robe,
he hastens the tilting of the hairs on the four seas;
he discourses upon the principle of quiescent extinction.
He preached the teachings on existence and non-existence,
opening the gateways of skillful means,
and expounded the twelve links of dependent origination.
The methods of guidance are manifold;
they expound the extensive teachings of the five thousand [stanzas].
By reverently following them, one carefree sojourns in the six perfections.
If one succumbs to negligence, one will flow forever through the ocean of suffering;
therefore, one shaves the beard and hair to become a śramaṇa,
casting off white robes to don black garments.
I hope to ascend to the other shore and emerge from this ford of craving;
my parents value my appearance,
and the princes and nobles revere my precepts.
This is precisely the way in which one is separated from ruler and kin, distancing oneself from the mundane and severing ties with the dusty world.
One is not constrained by the three hundred ritual observances,
nor does one harbor any longing for the rank of the five marquises.
It is not yet appropriate to earnestly exhort these customs or to encourage them through refined demeanor.
Let us bow our heads in private residences and prostrate ourselves before the public court;
we pray that you will follow the established precedent.
This is reasonable for the ignorant;
we respectfully submit this deliberation.

A memorial of the deliberations by Wang Quan, Giver of Audience at the Inner Attendants’ Office, Hu Xuanliang, Doctor, and others. A single memorial of the deliberations by Wang Quan, Giver of Audience at the Inner Attendants’ Office, Hu Xuanliang, Doctor, and others: We humbly consider that...
On Mount Qi he propagated the transformation,
rowing his oars across the hidden ford;
from the azure void he bestowed his instructions.
Turning toward the true realm,
he proclaimed that his virtue encompasses the four heavens;
his teachings stand out as extraordinary compared to worldly conventions.
The principle is uniform as a single finger,
yet the resources for veneration differ from ordinary norms; thus,
he performed the rites at the Forest of Firmness (Śrāvastī).
The ultimate principle and common sentiment follow different systems;
though he humbled himself by the banks of the River,
his profound efficacy already diverged from mundane affairs.
Thus we know that black robes and yellow caps are not the proper adornments for the imperial court; rather,
they belong to the Zen groves and mountain caves.
How could this alone be the glory of a minister or a son?
Rather, its merit is profound and its benefit vast; it fully encompasses the path of universal guidance.
It sets forth the principles of the Three Vehicles, reaching the ultimate truth for the four classes of living beings.
The text of five thousand words reveals that its discourse encompasses the myriad phenomena;
wielding the sword of wisdom to sever afflictions,
one abandons desire for existence and practices non-action.
The living and the dead look up to him as their vessel;
all things that move and grow depend upon him for their nourishment.
His nature and characteristics cannot be fully exhausted by the application of intellectual inquiry.
How could the profound mysteries of the "Invisible and the Unnameable" be exhausted by mere inquiry?
Moreover, since he turns the Wheel of Dharma to assist the sovereign’s merit,
his achievement shall save beings throughout the dust-motes of kalpas.
When the true qi floats upward to establish the foundation of the Sagely Way,
then the Way transcends the primordial chaos—
how vast, how great!
Truly, there is nothing by which it can be adequately praised.
Now, desiring that the teachings of the Name be made to conform to secular rites,
the imperial decree has already been issued.
Who would not say this is appropriate?
Yet I fear that, because of this, the spirit of noble refinement will gradually vanish,
and the profound and mysterious principles will drift away, lost to return.
We humbly submit that Your Majesty’s love and reverence surpass those of a hundred sovereigns,
and your virtuous governance extends throughout the four seas.
To concentrate the spirit, embody all things, and take the propagation of the Way as one's heart—
why must one restrict oneself to these two gates and conflate the paths of the ultimate and the conventional?
Restricting ourselves to these two teachings,
we have confused the paths of silence and speech;
since the precepts and regulations differ from the standard codes.
Prostrations on one's knees do not accord with ordinary etiquette;
as for the practice of following precedent,
I request that you adhere to the established norms.
Respectfully submitted for deliberation.

This memorial of deliberation by Liu Qingdao, Vice Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, Hao Chujie, Archivist, and others, states: Filial piety and nourishment are the means by which one serves one’s parents.
The hair and skin constitute the beginning of filial piety;
reverence and loyalty are the means by which one serves superiors.
Kneeling and prostrating are the outward expressions that extend the essence of respect.
This indeed involves looking upward to investigate the celestial ordinances and looking downward to exhaust the principles of human nature.
Yet, when it comes to the ultimate state of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and tranquil extinction (*nirvāṇa*), both speech and action come to an end;
it is profound, mysterious, rare, and subtle, so remote and dark as to be difficult to fathom. Your Majesty has expanded the Right Path and opened wide the Gate of Mystery.
Those who promote that Dharma receive this profound spiritual protection; yet,
the Teaching is not a matter of worldly governance,
for its form constitutes a ritual beyond the mundane realm.
Their clothing differs from that of other nations,
and their bodies lack head ornaments;
how can they participate with the gentry in the ritual of prostration?
In the privy, they used a hairpin and knelt with their bodies fully extended.
I, a fool, believe that those who succeed to the Dharma and emulate the sages may maintain their integrity and not bow their heads in court.
Having disfigured their appearance and severed [worldly ties],
they may thus dispense with the rites of deference due to kin;
moreover, they are of the same order as Chao Fu and Xu You.
It is beneficial for the flourishing of virtuous deeds and the fulfillment of entrusted mandates; thus,
one should persistently cultivate goodness.
Having received Your Majesty’s enlightened decree,
I venture to present this orthodox argument.
Respectfully submitted for deliberation.

A Memorial on the Deliberations of Wang Qianshi, Assistant Director of the Ministry of Judicial Review, Zhang Daoxun, Rectifier, and Others. We, Wang Qianshi, Assistant Director of the Ministry of Judicial Review, and Zhang Daoxun, Rectifier, humbly consider the matter as follows.
The bond between sovereign and subject is profound;
the principles of loyalty and filial piety are fundamentally exalted.
The affection between father and son is deep.
The feelings of love and reverence are most earnest;
they preserve the principles of daily life and bear witness to the great grace of creation and sustenance.
How could those who receive its shade ever forget its virtue?
How could those who partake of its bounty...
It would rather be better to omit the ritual;
this is indeed consistent with the profound instructions on the three fundamental relationships and serves as a model for uniformity.
Thus, the principle accords with the divine intent, and the meaning conforms to the sacred edict.
However, the laws within the secular realm differ from those of Laozi and Śākyamuni,
and the tracks beyond the world diverge from those of Yao and Confucius; thus,
even the metaphors of the fish-trap and the rabbit-snare cannot fully convey this.
Both nature and characteristics are extinguished;
it is not constrained by the Small or the Great.
Heaven and earth are unified as one.
One does not regard the nourishment of the physical form as filial piety,
nor does one harbor doubt regarding the abandonment of kin;
the Way of the Spirits endures for a long time.
If one does not cease at this point,
but seeks its essential purport,
it will likewise assist in the transformation of beings.
Therefore, they wear unconventional dress without violating established regulations,
and they alter their physical appearance without harming the principles of the teachings;
thus they transcend the mundane world.
He is a guest of unrestrained freedom;
profound yet without decline,
he stands majestic, perfectly serene.
Although cause and effect are difficult to comprehend and the ultimate principle is profound and obscure—
seeming both to exist and to vanish.
This has been the case since ancient times.
In the past, Shi Yuan composed a treatise and Yu Xitan of the Jin dynasty engaged in discourse;
they both promoted such negligence.
It is better to honor their reverence.
Now, if you revere their Way while destroying their Dharma, and seek their blessings while subjecting your own person to humiliation; [this would be a grave error].
This causes those who strike their sounding staffs to adopt the dignified bearing of one wearing a sword and jade pendants,
while those who hold incense burners and upright their hairpins and tablets observe the rites of official decorum;
thus, both the monastic and the lay stand side by side.
In practicing these two acts of respectful giving,
the *kāṣāya* robe puts to shame the majesty of the golden-winged Garuda,
and the alms bowl puts to shame the incantations of the dragon-subduing sorcerer.
As for this teaching, where could it possibly be applied? We, Xun and the others,
have already humbly disgraced ourselves by being counted among the commoners’ humble advice.
I am unworthy to offer such a selection;
I have nonetheless ventured to set forth my humble views.
I remain deeply apprehensive and fearful.
Respectfully deliberated.

A memorial of the deliberations by Liang Xiaoren, Minister of the Ministry of Agriculture, Zhao Xingben, Director of the Grand Granary Bureau, and others: The rise of Buddhism and Daoism dates back to ancient times.
From the time the white light shone from the east and the purple qi drifted from the west,
there have been none who have not followed those five thousand words and revered these two teachings.
Through non-action and tranquil extinction, all together plant the seeds of supreme causes.
Furthermore, monks, nuns, Daoists, and female officials attend to and uphold their respective canons and teachings;
as for their doctrines,
they provide substantial assistance and benefit.
Examining the works of former masters, there were certainly instances of what was accepted and what was rejected;
thus, the fact that they collectively adhered to the practice of not prostrating is indeed worthy of observation.
As for the Way as the fundamental principle, the foundation of the empire is established through gradual stages.
The urgency of their dignity differs from that of ordinary people;
how could one alter their ritual to humbly conform to common custom?
To persist in not bowing is, in principle, deemed appropriate.
Respectfully submitted for deliberation.

A memorial on the proposal by Wei Siji, Minister of the Court of Exchequer, Jia Ju, Archivist, and others. Regarding the memorial on the proposal by Wei Siji, Minister of the Court of Exchequer, Jia Ju, Archivist, and others: We humbly consider that...
It is indeed the established rule for ministers and sons to prostrate themselves; however,
within the ritual classics there are also provisions for exceptional circumstances,
such as a mother bowing to her son.
One becomes a full person through ritual propriety;
one does not serve as a minister to such a ruler,
thereby honoring the Way and its Virtue.
How much more so for the teachings beyond the secular world;
their ways of practicing goodness differ,
and their paths transcend the void.
The Buddha is without birth or extinction;
one cultivates the mind and refines practice,
relying upon cause and effect.
This is called "leaving home" (renunciation).
Its brilliance transcends the mundane world, and all declare it a supreme practice.
Honored by successive dynasties, it has established flourishing sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍas).
All seek eternal bliss;
they present offerings to their sovereigns and parents to broaden their merit,
and rescue all sentient beings from the dark paths of existence.
For a long time, we have argued that [the Buddhist teachings] are superior to worldly doctrines;
yet, if they were treated as being on the same footing as Confucianism, they would merely re-enter the ranks of the secular.
Without venerating the disciples of learning, there would be no means by which the Way could be manifested.
It is solely due to their reverent protection that the Way remains perpetually extant.
The ritual of not prostrating serves to manifest profound guardianship;
the foundation of honoring the Way takes the pursuit of benefit as its primary principle.
Now, according to the scriptural text, it says:
"Prostration does not benefit people or profit the state;
this is truly what should be said."
How could I dare to present writings that offer no benefit?
To follow the law while maintaining the old ways ensures that the established statutes remain without deficiency;
to embody the subtle and exhaust the profound is something beyond the reach of those below.
Fortunate to have been graced with the opportunity to offer these humble deliberations,
I venture to exhaust my foolish sincerity,
yet I fear they may not be appropriate.
I am deeply grieved and apprehensive and respectfully submit this deliberation.

A Memorandum on the Construction Project by Liu Shenli, Chief Supervisor of the Office of Works, and Supervising Officials including the Turks, etc., consisting of one item: Regarding Monks and Nuns. I have privately observed that the Sovereign reveres the spirits and deities.
The various classes of deities revere the disciples of the Buddha;
therefore, to clarify their distant respect,
they honor what is honorable by bowing and performing ritual salutations.

I, the fool, say this is not yet permissible. A certain monk saw an official receive an imperial edict and did not bow; he did so not because the royal teacher was inferior or beneath him, but because he respected the sovereign’s teachings. Monastic clergy dye their robes and shave their hair to distinguish their form from the laity; they receive the Buddha’s decree to cultivate blessings for the state. They pay reverence to the sovereign and their parents, but do not prostrate before their own persons; as monks for the sake of the Dharma-robe, they do not bow to the sovereign or their parents.
First, I have observed that the divine image stands there because people fashioned its form;
once the form was completed, people returned to revere it.
How could it be that because [the status] is established by others, it does not attain the highest honor?
If it does not attain the highest honor, what is the use of establishing it at all?
The Buddha entrusted his final teachings to the kings.
That which the King establishes, the King himself honors and respects.
If the King does not show respect, what benefit is there in establishing it?
Monk; nun-monk; monk; nun-monk.
I have observed that those who succeed the former dynasties stand at the head of a hundred kings; likewise,
the Daoist masters personally don the ritual vestments of the Lord Lao.
The oral tradition transmits the Dharma-words of the Old Lord (Laojun).
To prostrate in accordance with secular custom would,
I fear, violate the proper ritual.
Respectfully submitted for deliberation.

A memorial on the proposal by Linghu Defen, Grand Director of the Office of Imperial Education, and others. We, Linghu Defen, Grand Director of the Office of Imperial Education, and others, humbly submit this memorial: We have observed that the two teachings of Śākyamuni and the Buddha are profound and vast in their compassion and reverence.
There are countries where, through long-standing custom, a tradition of veneration has been established;
having persisted for so long, their laws must follow that path.
Yet, I venture to say that the principle of prostration is likely not yet fully understood.
How can shaving the head compare to the rites of cap and sash?
How can holding an alms bowl be the ritual of the sacrificial vessels and stands?
To extend grace, one should simply pray for concentration and wisdom; there is no need for laborious formality.
Prostrating and kneeling before one's venerable parents, one hopes to repay their kindness;
why must one truly bend the waist for a compassionate sovereign?
Once the mountain forests have been left behind, [the path is clear].
No longer a guest of the imperial court,
the distinction between the capital and the provinces is now merely formal;
it is only right that he should hold his noble pursuits as paramount.
If we are now held accountable for failing in the principles of the Name-teachings (mingjiao),
we, your humble and ignorant subjects,
beg leave that it be appropriate for us to follow the practice of not bowing.
Respectfully submitted for deliberation.
A Memorandum of Deliberation by the Director of the National Academy, the Keeper of the Hall of Propagation of Learning, Fan Yiyun, and others. Your Servant has heard: [text continues]
The Ultimate Way is profound and empty;
Prajñā is mysterious and still.
In relation to humanity, it is what makes a person venerable.
In whatever place one dwells, that place becomes noble.
Thus, the Immortal Laozi of the River descended to the lofty heights of Empress Liu;
and the renowned monks of Chicken Peak humbled themselves before the great honor of the Cakravartin King.
Thus we know that this custom has long been prevalent and has been followed by all for a thousand years.
According to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other scriptures,
such is the dharma for those who have left the household life.
One does not prostrate before kings or parents;
even those who transmit the Confucian teachings still maintain a formal equality with sovereigns, exchanging courtesies on equal terms.
The grandson serves as the ancestral representative (shi), and when the eldest son receives the cap and the inheritance, his parents still bow to him;
this is to ensure the transmission of the lineage’s weight.
Today, our Sage Ruler models himself after the yielding and ceding of Yao and Shun.
He allowed Rén Yáng and Xǔ You to remain non-officials;
he surpassed Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn in his magnanimity and benevolence;
and he permitted the Four Elders to dwell beyond the mundane world.
How much more so for one who has received the entrustment to propagate and expound the profound teachings!
Since you have been permitted to leave the household life, it is only logical that you should remain secluded from worldly affairs.
To suddenly dispatch you to pay court is truly a matter of great astonishment and suspicion.
To set aside the law for the sake of employing individuals—
this, I consider, is not yet permissible.
Furthermore, the *Li* says:
One who is acting as an intermediary does not prostrate,
for that would cause him to lose his proper deportment and measure.
Those who have left the mundane world wear the armor of patience upon their bodies.
Now, to follow the common custom of kneeling is to demean the court protocol.
Having been honored by holding office in the Upper School and mistakenly participating in the halls of the worthy,
I have received profound grace.
I venture to set forth my humble views. Respectfully submitted for deliberation.

A Memorial on the Deliberations of Zhang Yanshi, General of the Left Guard, and Others. We, Zhang Yanshi, General of the Left Guard, and others, humbly submit this memorial: We have considered that...
The profound mysteries of Laozi unfold the gateway to all wonders;
the tranquil stillness of the Buddhist teachings [is likewise].
A realm of carefree transcendence from the mundane.
Since the Golden Countenance crossed to the East and the True Breath roamed to the West, those who draw near the Way and aspire to its breeze have filled every region and domain.
As the Sage Dynasty has governed the course of fortune, this Way has flourished even more greatly.
Benevolent shrines and Dharma halls stand magnificent throughout the capital;
jeweled banners and golden spires dazzle the thoroughfares.
All these offerings are intended to provide spiritual sustenance and benefit, while simultaneously preserving the teachings.
I humbly believe this may be reconciled;
I respectfully submit this deliberation.

The memorial on the proposal by Cui Xiuye, Chief Steward of the Right Guard, and others, states: "The principles and purports of the two teachings of Li [Confucianism] and Shi [Buddhism] are profound and deep."
Its principle transcends names and words, and its merit surpasses the realm of thought.
The Way takes purity as its essence;
the Buddha takes the salvation of sentient beings as his primary concern.
Thus, he serves as a bridge for all sentient beings and shall lead those with form to the other shore;
for this reason, he humbled himself before Emperor Wen of Wei on the banks of the river.
On Vulture Peak, he moved Emperor Minghuang;
from that time onward, his Way became ever more widespread,
reaching as far as the subtle principles beneath the pillar and the divine traces in Kāśī.
Those who look up to its Way do not recognize its ultimate destination;
those who draw from its waves...
Without detailed accounts of his beginning and end,
we shall now examine how he mounted his cranes to roam the Five Ridges and manifested his forms throughout the three thousand worlds.
This is truly a case of manifesting through provisional traces as an emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) to skillfully guide and receive others;
those who rely upon this transformation all aspire to the merit of ascending lightly to the heavens.
Those who supported his practice were likewise rescued throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust; thus,
once the yellow caps were changed and the black robes had barely moistened their bodies.
A sovereign does not bend before his ministers,
nor do parents treat their children as mere livestock;
this is how one honors the Buddha-way.
It is not that this violates the rules of propriety;
what harm does bowing and saluting do to the body?
I only fear it may cause a deficiency in the sacred teachings.
It is essential that both form and spirit be simultaneously cast aside and bowing and saluting be mutually forgotten;
being equally one with that Heavenly Truth,
there is no need for the humiliation of formal courtesy.
Since the nature and characteristics have not yet been fully exhausted,
they remain as if existent and yet non-existent;
in principle, one must accomplish these supreme causes to fulfill such noble aspirations.
Moreover, the present Sage Emperor, reverent and enlightened, governs the world with filial piety;
he especially honors the two teachings to support the field of merit.
For this reason, he permits the Daoist masters and Buddhist monks not to prostrate themselves.
Furthermore, it would be very easy to send [him] to pay homage, yet very difficult not to pay homage;
this would enable even a young child in the fields of Xiang to excel not only the Emperor Xuan.
The old man by the river does not monopolize the credit for beauty that belongs to Emperor Han;
that "one gain from a thousand deliberations" is surely worthy of being honored.
Respectfully submitted for deliberation.

This is the memorial on the proposal of Wang Xuance, Chief Secretary of the Right Cavalry Guard, Xiao Guan of the Cavalry Office, and others. Regarding the memorial on the proposal of Wang Xuance, Chief Secretary of the Right Cavalry Guard, Xiao Guan of the Cavalry Office, and others: Since the rise of Buddhism, it has originated in India.
Your servant has had considerable experience through three previous missions.
Your servant has heard that King Śuddhodana is the father of the Buddha,
and Mahāmāyā is the mother of the Buddha.
The monk Upāli was originally a servant of the royal household;
the king personally paid him universal homage and respect as he did for the Buddha.
Furthermore, the minister observed the monastic discipline of the monks and nuns in that country.
They do not prostrate before the shrines of various celestial deities,
nor do they prostrate before kings or their parents; rather,
both kings and parents all pay homage to the monks and nuns, as well as to the various members of the Daoist community.
I once challenged that monk, saying:
"This servant has only recently shaved his head and donned the black robes;
he possesses no knowledge whatsoever."
"To immediately command your father to pay you homage is utterly contrary to human feeling.
The monk replied:
Although his appearance was already identical to that of a Buddha from the moment his hair was first shaved,
he was further able to shake the palaces of Māra.
Though said to be without consciousness, how could he be any different from clay or wood?
A single piece of carved wood standing upright serves as the image of the Master;
even those who are powerful, noble, and eminent do not fail to pay their respects.
That monks do not bow to the laity is thus clearly established.
Another minister further challenged that monk, saying:
"In the Vimalakīrti Sūtra,
it is said that a bhikṣu also prostrates at the feet of Vimalakīrti."
The Lotus Sūtra and the *Sengxing pujing* (The Universal Veneration of the Sangha)—
the texts of these two sūtras.
"It is clear that one should bow to the laity.
For what reason, then, may a bhikṣu not bow to a venerable elder?
The Saṃgha replied:
The Vinaya-sūtras prescribed by the Buddha constitute the constant rule for monks and nuns;
as for the Vimalakīrti-sūtra, it describes a bhikṣu upholding the Dharma who temporarily performs a formal salutation.
"The *Lotus Sūtra* was practiced separately by Great Beings at one time.
How can you use such temporary, separate practices to confound this eternal canon?
The subject deeply agreed with this.
I have heard that when his wife died, Zhuangzi beat a basin for a drum and sang around her corpse.
This was merely an extraordinary act performed on a single occasion;
how could it possibly be included within the regulations for mourning attire?
A certain official once performed a ritual prostration before a celestial image in India;
the king there then smiled and asked him:
The messengers were all upāsakas;
for what reason did they pay homage to the gods?
The minister asked for the reason behind this.
The answer is:
According to the dharma of these upāsakas, they do not prostrate to devas.
Formerly, King Kaniṣka received the five precepts from the Buddha.
He also prostrated before the celestial images,
and all the images fell to the ground.
Finally, he reached the image of the Sun God (Sūrya).
The one who performed the rites for the deity feared that when the King arrived, the image of the deity would fall over during the ritual prostrations.
He therefore secretly placed the Buddha image atop the deity's head.
When the King performed his three prostrations, the image did not fall.
The king, finding this strange, ordered an inspection.
Within the crown, they discovered a Buddha image.
The king was greatly delighted and marveled at the divine majesty of the Buddha.
Appreciating his wisdom, he was highly rewarded with a fief,
which remains extant to this day.
It is further said:
There was a non-Buddhist who had received the five precepts from the Buddha;

Furthermore, the reliance upon human effort in matters of prosperity and decline is likewise evident here: Your Majesty, exercising discernment and seizing the opportune moment, has truly fulfilled the mandate of trust.

The *Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chunqiu Zhuan) states:
"If that which the ruler deems acceptable contains elements of what is unacceptable,
the minister shall present those unacceptable elements so as to perfect the acceptability."
"In what Your Majesty calls 'no,' there may yet be something 'yes.

I have heard these words before.

Guān Xiù has exerted his utmost efforts in composing the "Explanatory Statement for the Ruler" (*Shìjùn Chāngyán*); his words and intentions presented to the imperial court are sincere and earnest.
While his diligence is indeed praiseworthy, the memorial submitted by Master Xuán is detailed, incisive, comprehensive, and profound.
I have no hesitation in this matter.
At present, I take it upon myself the great Dharma,
intending to rectify its decline and peril.
"One who can bear heavy burdens and travel long distances—
is this not such a person? Thus spoke Zhongni."
If one is staggering and not supported,
or in peril and not sustained,

If this is truly so, it may be called the pinnacle of supreme enlightenment.
How excellent!
This deliberation by the ministers, the central government, and the various departments is indeed commendable.
Although their literary style and substance may differ, both capture the essential points of the matter. Yet,
as they consult the subtle pivot of the scriptures and investigate ancient precedents,
their principles and examples are sharp and incisive, while their diction and rhythm are rich and nourishing.
Thus, the title "Director of Military Affairs" (Sirong) is indeed characterized by grand brushwork and elegant diction.
If one were to highlight it with manifest arguments and summarize it with rectitude,
its phrasing would be literary and eloquent, while its matters would be clear and substantiated.
Thus, the Left Cavalry Guard has grasped its essential principles.
Those who come after shall find their guidance therein; from this, they shall take it all.
The eulogy says:
Since the True Dharma has been obscured and the Age of the Counterfeit Dharma has become faint,
were it not for those of brilliant wisdom, [the teachings would surely perish].
Who shall cause the sun of wisdom to shine?
May you present what is right and replace what is wrong,
so that its brilliance may soar and its fruits may gather.
Examining the worthies of antiquity in detail and verifying it against the present day,
they were all exceptionally eminent and outstanding.
This was to shake loose the fallen cords of order.
Duke Xuan, with resolute integrity,
upheld the Mandate and rectified the state.
The deliberations of the assembly were resonant and harmonious;
the grand counsels were bold and upright.
Like orchids and chrysanthemums, they each possessed distinct beauties.
While the strings and the zither alternate in performance,
Master Qin’s grand brush and Master Wang’s brilliant arguments unfold.
Cultivation and substance diverge in their paths,
yet loyalty and integrity are equally sublime;
such is this magnificent virtue.
His plans were without fail excellent;
his pure character of that time has spread its fragrance for a thousand years.

The six positions manifest the image of the lofty distinction between high and low;
they are the root of a hundredfold conduct.
The four beginnings proclaim the discourse on boundless gratitude.
Only when the foundation is established does the Way arise.
Reverence manifests therein, and ritual becomes harmonious; this is truly the beginning of the royal transformation and the fundamental principle of Heaven and Earth.
The Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher;
the Emperor takes Heaven as his model.
Within the realm, there are four great things.
The sovereign occupies one of these positions;
once the Way of the King has reached parity,
the laws will naturally follow as a single thread.
As one who is a vessel for the Dharma, the Dharma alone is the root of the Way.
Those in yellow caps admire the Way, while those in black robes revere the Buddha.
To pay homage to the sovereign and father is to have a subtle resonance with the profound waves [of the Dharma]. Thus he said:
The Buddha-dharma is the most honored beyond the world;

Yet, while the teachings remain, they are forced to submit and lose their independence, becoming no different from those bound by the commoners' code.

How could there be a profound resonance with the mysterious waves? Furthermore, when the records of the precepts are merely elevated, one still exerts oneself to the utmost in reverent prostrations.

For when the fundamental principles are identical,

Truly profound are these words;

To bestow favor upon me would not be for this purpose;

Tranquil and eternally quiescent, he abides in the provisional;

I request that you immediately include this in the permanent statutes; what shortcoming have you observed? If it were thus, the advancement of virtue, the cultivation of practice, and the path for transcending the mundane would flourish ever more greatly.

Now, what is it that defines one as a śramaṇa?
It means to succeed to the Dharma, emulate the sages, enlighten the ignorant, and initiate transformation.
Their outward appearance differs from the finery of court officials, and their teachings diverge from the regulations of the imperial court.
Because they seek the ultimate principle, they leave their physical remains behind;
who could divide their virtuous achievements?
Because they rectify worldly customs, they thereby maintain a stance of ritual independence.

How can it be permitted to separate [the practice] based on status? Whether at home or in the state, when serving a ruler or one's parents, how can such a ritual of not bowing serve as a model for instruction? He rebuked him, saying: [The text continues with the rebuke: "The Master of the Left, Xun Xu, has submitted a memorial stating that 'the rites of the Three Dynasties were simple and easy to follow, while those of the Five Dynasties were complex and difficult to implement. This is a grave error. The rites of the Three Dynasties were indeed simple and easy to follow because they were rooted in the human heart; the rites of the Five Dynasties were complex and difficult to implement because they were merely external forms.

Now, if you take the simplicity of the Three Dynasties as a standard and reject the complexity of the Five Dynasties, you are effectively discarding the rites of the Five Dynasties and reverting to the crude customs of the barbarians. Furthermore, you cite the example of Duke Wen of Jin, who did not bow to his mother. However, this was a specific instance where he declined to bow out of filial piety, not a general rule for all. To take such an isolated case as a universal principle is to distort the meaning of the classics. [End of quote.]
Truly, for those who serve their sovereign and parents, it is inappropriate not to perform prostrations.

That śramaṇas do not serve kings or lords, turning their backs on the natural bond of kinship and taking prostration as their instruction, seems to stem from a lack of reflection. We hope you will issue a decree prohibiting such prostrations.
To establish a model for posterity.
Respectfully submitted for deliberation.
A Memorial by Zhang Songshou, Magistrate of Chang’an County. One Memorial by Zhang Songshou, Magistrate of Chang’an County. I humbly consider as follows:
The two gates of Buddhahood and the Way are one in their emptiness and stillness.
Even if one cannot refine the mind beyond the mundane world or cast off one’s shadow from among men,
one must at least keep one’s traces distinct from the secular.
The events are now separated by time.
Yet, those who have left the household life today are for the most part mixed among the ranks of the mundane.
Outwardly, they exalt themselves through stubborn refusal to conform.
Internally, they made private audiences their primary concern;
they possessed only the reputation of entering the Way, yet ultimately lacked the reality of renouncing worldly life. Criticism states: [as follows].
Those who do not yield serve the Dharma with sincerity;

those who seek private audiences truly violate the principles of the teachings. One may only strictly enforce regulations to punish such unruly elements; how could one tolerate setting fire to Mount Kunlun, intending for both jade and stone to be consumed by the flames?
As for the sphere of sovereign and parent, the rites encompass both minister and son;
where filial piety and reverence are the primary principles, the significance extends deeply to family and state.
Without established institutions, how could one manage the affairs of governance?
I request that monks, nuns, Daoist masters, female officials,
and others take this as their duty for the sake of the times;
whenever there is a need arising from a dharma assembly, they must attend.
Although they are in the presence of the sovereign and the consort, let them follow the established protocol;
from this point forward, I request that they all be required to prostrate.
If they return to visit their parents, the way of a son should be fully observed.
As in the case of visiting a temple, one should follow the scriptural precedents.
[The Master] rebuked him, saying:

"If monks and nuns are required to bow to one another, it would be improper not to do so; yet if they are not required to bow, why restrict this based on time or place? How can it be that those who have shaved their heads are considered the same person, such that the rule is waived simply because of their location?"
To maintain different ritual codes and robes from beginning to end without any change is,
in effect, to act like a rat caught between two ends;
it is merely a contrivance to seek temporal reputation.
It is said that his aspirations were lofty, serving his family and state with loyalty and integrity; he likely regarded base submission as a source of shame.
He gradually distanced himself from frivolous competition, honoring himself through the Way and its Virtue.
